## 1\. Project Purpose

The project will produce a practical, low cost, and demo friendly system for tracking Industry 4.0 assets even in areas without GPS. Our focus will be on designing this prototype at low cost, proving the concept works, collecting useful data, analyzing it, and showing how this could support Industry 4.0 asset tracking and recovery.

## 2\. Challenge

Factories, construction sites, shipping yards, and warehouses can lose time and money when tools, equipment, and valuable inventory are misplaced, lost or stolen. GPS can help outside, but it becomes unreliable indoors, near metal structures, inside containers, trailers, underground, or in other areas where GPS is unavailable.

High-end tracking systems exist, but they can be expensive, require cellular subscriptions, satellite plans, or need a lot of fixed infrastructure. This project explores a simpler, cheaper option that could fit smaller teams, temporary job sites or facilities that want useful, low-cost, private tracking without a large system rollout.

# 3\. Recommended Solution

The recommended solution is a two-part system:

* Hider tag: a small RF tracker attached to the asset. It sends location, status, and sensor data over LoRa or Bluetooth.  
* Seeker receiver: a handheld or dashboard-based receiver that listens for the Hider, shows the last known location, and helps guide the user toward the tag.

When GPS is available, the Hider sends its current GPS location. When GPS is not available, the Hider sends its last known GPS location and switches into Marco Polo Mode. In Marco Polo Mode, it sends repeated RF chirps so the Seeker can guide the user with a simple hotter-colder search.

For testing, the Hider may include a simple No GPS switch. This lets us simulate an indoor or GPS-denied area even if the tag can still see GPS during the demo.

# 4\. Main Use Cases

* Construction site asset recovery: A generator, tool box, or equipment case is moved around a job site. When it is outside, it reports GPS. When it is inside a building or trailer, it switches to recovery chirps.  
* Warehouse or inventory tracking: A tagged bin or cart reports its location when possible. If GPS is unavailable, the Seeker uses RF signal strength to narrow down where it is.  
* Manufacturing tool tracking: A calibration tool, fixture, or inventory bin can report status and help workers recover it if it is misplaced.  
* Class demo: The team hides with the Hider and another team uses the Seeker to follow the signal trend until the tag is found.  Hard mode has the GPS switch turned off for foxhunting.

# 5\. Project Scope

The project will be built in phases so the team has a realistic minimum version and several possible stretch goals.

Minimum viable prototype:

* Send simple LoRa or Bluetooth packets from the Hider to the Seeker.  
* Show tag ID, mode, GPS location, packet count, and basic received signal information.  
* Collect a small dataset from test runs, including packet success, signal trends, and recovery time.  
* Use the TinyML kit and its sensors to collect motion, orientation, vibration, or disturbance data.

Planned next phase:

* Add GPS-lost Marco Polo Mode with last known GPS and repeated chirps.  
* Add a Seeker view that shows map/location information, RSSI, status, and hotter-colder guidance.

Stretch goals:

* Use a Raspberry Pi and touch display for a cleaner Seeker interface.  
* Overlay the data on a map/floor plan.  
* Use Unity for a simple simulation or visualization layer.  
* 3D print a custom enclosure for the tag or Seeker.  
* Build or test a low-cost directional antenna for better foxhunting.  
* Connect the Seeker to a robot so it can move toward the Hider automatically.

# 6\. TinyML, Sensors, Data Collection, and Analysis

The TinyML kit is a required part of the project and will be used as an edge sensor and classification platform. The team will collect sensor data and use it to describe the asset state.

Possible sensor inputs include:

* GPS availability, GPS coordinates, and last known location.  
* LoRa or Bluetooth packet counts, packet loss, latency, and signal trend data.  
* TinyML sensor readings such as motion, orientation, vibration, or impact events.  
* Recovery time during Marco Polo test runs.

The analysis will stay simple. The team will look at whether the Seeker reliably receives packets, whether the Hider can report useful location/status data, whether Marco Polo Mode helps recovery, and whether sensor/TinyML data adds useful context.

# 7\. System Approach and Interfaces

The system will follow a simple flow:

**Hider sensors and GPS \-\> LoRa/BLE packet \-\> Seeker receiver \-\> display or dashboard \-\> data log \-\> analysis \-\> optional directional antenna or robot action.**

Physical interfaces may include the TinyML/BLE Sense board, LoRa modules, GPS module, antennas, battery, Raspberry Pi display, 3D printed shell, and optional robot platform.

Programmatic interfaces may include serial data, LoRa packets, BLE messages, CSV or JSON logs, TinyML classification output, dashboard visualization, possible Unity input, and optional robot commands.

# 8\. Cost Estimate

The project will use already-owned and class-provided hardware as much as possible. The new cash cost should stay fairly low, but the total project cost should also include the value of labor because this is still engineering work.

Estimated hardware and material cost:

* Hider system (LoRa, GPS, TinyML, battery, and antenna): about $50  
* Seeker system (LoRa, GPS, Arduino, screen, battery, and antenna): about $75  
* Optional Raspberry Pi \+ display, enclosure filament, extra antennas, and small parts: about $140

Estimated out-of-pocket cost if starting from scratch is about $125 for the base system

For the stretch goal system the total amount would likely be around $265.

Estimated labor cost: assuming 4 team members, about 25 hours each, at a simple graduate engineering project rate of $30/hour. That is 100 hours x $30 \= $3,000.

**Estimated total project cost including labor: about $3,125 to $3,265.**

This estimate is intentionally rough. The prototype is designed for a low per-unit cost, but the engineering time needed to design, build, test, analyze, and document it make a higher non-recurring engineering (NRE) cost.

# 9\. Schedule Estimate

* Week 1-2: Team charter, project charter, architecture, and first LoRa communication test.  
* Week 2-3: Add GPS reporting or simulated GPS packets. Define packet format and logging.  
* Week 3-4: Collect TinyML sensor data and connect asset state to Hider/Seeker behavior.  
* Week 4-6: Add GPS-lost Marco Polo Mode and basic hotter-colder recovery testing.  
* Week 6-7: Add visualization, dashboard, Raspberry Pi display, floor plan, or Unity view if realistic.  
* Week 7-8: Analyze data, clean up demo, write results, and prepare final presentation.

# 10\. Quality Targets

* The Hider should send readable packets to the Seeker.  
* The Seeker should show the Hider state in a way a normal user can understand.  
* GPS location sharing should work outdoors or with clear sky exposure.  
* GPS-lost mode should clearly show last known location plus recovery chirps.  
* TinyML or sensor logic should clearly connect to the asset recovery story.  
* The team should save enough data to support basic analysis and final reporting.

# 11\. Main Risks

Weather and natural events. Outdoor GPS and LoRa testing can be affected by rain, lightning, heat, wind, storms, or local emergencies. Natural disasters or severe weather could also make outdoor testing unsafe or delay access to test areas.

* Mitigation: do not test outdoors in unsafe weather. Use bench tests, simulated GPS-lost mode, recorded data, and indoor tests when outdoor testing is not practical. Keep schedule buffer for field tests.

LoRa versus Bluetooth risk. Bluetooth is easier and is already available on the TinyML/BLE Sense board, but its range is limited and it does not fully prove the long-range recovery concept. LoRa better matches the project goal because it supports longer-range, low-power packets, but it creates more technical risk.

* LoRa risk is higher because radio configuration, antenna choice, packet format, GPS integration, power, and RSSI/direction finding may be harder than expected.  
* Bluetooth risk is lower for a short-range demo, but higher for market fit because BLE may not work well for large sites or outdoor recovery unless more infrastructure is added.  
* Mitigation: use Bluetooth as a fallback or supporting channel, but keep LoRa as the main long-range tracking path if it works reliably.

Knowledge gaps. The project touches several areas that may need learning during the semester.

* RF/LoRa configuration and antennas.  
* GPS parsing, lock time, and location accuracy.  
* TinyML data collection and model evaluation.  
* Node-RED, dashboards, SQLite/logging, or mapping tools.  
* Power management and battery behavior.  
* Optional robot integration or Unity visualization.  
* Mitigation: test each subsystem early, keep the packet format simple, document issues, and protect the minimum demo before adding stretch goals.

Other risks include late hardware arrival, online-team integration issues, noisy RF signals, weak GPS indoors, and scope creep. The team will manage these by keeping the MVP small, dividing work into modules, and treating directional antenna, Raspberry Pi display, Unity, and robot recovery as optional stretch goals.

# 12\. Expected Results

The expected result is a working proof of concept that shows how a low-cost smart tag could support asset tracking and recovery in Industry 4.0 environments.

The final demo should show at least one asset tag communicating with a Seeker, sensor or TinyML data being collected, and a basic recovery workflow. The team should also produce a small dataset and analysis showing what worked, what did not, and what would be improved in a future version.

If time allows, the project may also show a better Seeker visualization, a floor plan or Unity view, a 3D printed enclosure, a directional antenna, or robot-assisted movement toward the tag.
